options.text: `$qty` should be a float, not an int
options.why: The opposite. The integer is fine; the problem is that the price is a float.

options.text: Nothing is wrong, 24.60 will match just fine

questions.q: How should $1,250.50 be stored in the database?

options.text: `1250.5` in a DOUBLE column
options.why: DOUBLE is a float; it stores approximations.

options.text: `125050` cents in a BIGINT column, with `USD` in a separate column
options.why: An integer minor unit is exact, and with the currency beside it the amount has a clear meaning.

options.text: `"1250.50"` in a VARCHAR column
options.why: You can't add or subtract strings, and formats can break.

options.text: `1250` dollars and `50` cents in two separate columns
options.why: When adding, you have to handle the carry yourself once the cents pass 100; a single integer is much simpler.

questions.q: Which is the biggest problem in this Money code?
questions.hint: What happens if you add an EUR Money to a USD Money?

options.text: It adds the two amounts without checking that the currencies match
options.why: USD 100 + EUR 5 would quietly become USD 105. You have to check the currencies and throw an exception before adding.

options.text: The method should not be `public`
options.why: A public add is fine; the problem is the missing currency check.

options.text: It creates a new Money, which is wrong
options.why: Returning a new object is exactly the right rule for an immutable value object.

options.text: The amount should be a `string`, not an `int`
options.why: An integer is the right choice; with a string you would have to cast again to add.

questions.q: Which of these are part of a sound Money design?
questions.hint: Think about the amount, the currency and overflow.

options.text: Storing the amount as an integer minor unit
options.why: Whole-number arithmetic has no approximation error.

options.text: Keeping the currency in the same object as the amount
options.why: If they are separate, the wrong pair can get stuck together; kept together, they can be matched before adding.

options.text: Catching overflow with `is_int` after the addition
options.why: PHP makes a float when an int overflows; this check stops the silent error.

options.text: Using a `float $amount` for convenience
options.why: The float is the root of the problem; there is no convenience, only hidden errors.

questions.q: $100 (10000 cents) is allocated among 3 people in the ratio 1:1:1. Which result is correct?

options.why: The total is 9999; 1 cent has gone missing.
The total is 10002; 2 cents were created from nothing.
The 1 cent remainder went to one person, and the total is exactly 10000.

options.why: The ledger has no such place, so the books won't balance later. The remainder has to go into someone's share.

questions.hint: What information would support use to find what was deducted?

options.text: Prove nothing; only the current amount exists, with no history
options.why: Each UPDATE erased the previous amount. Who lowered it, when and why can no longer be known.

options.text: Read the balance column's log to reconstruct the full history
options.why: A column has no log. If you add a separate log, that log is a ledger.

options.text: Look at the database's `updated_at` to learn the reason
options.why: It only tells you the time of the last change, not the reason or the amount.

options.text: Compare against the previous day's backup and find everything
options.why: A backup is a once-a-day snapshot; it doesn't contain what happened within the day.

questions.q: Which of these are sound ledger design choices?

options.text: The amount is always positive, with the direction in a separate `side` column
options.why: It avoids confusion over the direction of a negative amount.

options.text: The app's DB user is not granted UPDATE/DELETE on the entry table
options.why: History can't change, even through a bug or a rush.

options.text: The balance is checked against the entries regularly
options.why: If a cached balance and the sum of entries differ, the error is caught; the entries are the right ones.

options.text: It should compare with `==` instead of `!==`
options.why: The comparison operator is not the problem; what is being compared is.

options.text: It should throw only when `$debits` is larger than `$credits`

questions.hint: Each currency needs its own matching pair.

options.text: Ryan D 625 USD, FX USD C 625 USD, FX GBP D 500 GBP, Kevin C 500 GBP
options.why: USD: 625 = 625. GBP: 500 = 500. Each currency balances on its own.

options.text: Ryan D 625 USD, Kevin C 500 GBP
options.why: USD nets to +625 and GBP to -500; neither balances.

options.text: Ryan D 625 USD, Kevin C 625 GBP
options.why: It balances as plain numbers, but Kevin would receive 625 pounds, not 500.

options.text: missing_in_ledger; find the cause and write a correcting entry

options.text: missing_at_provider; refund the customer
options.why: Here the gateway does have the transaction, so this is not missing_at_provider.

questions.q: Which of these make good matching keys for reconciliation?

options.text: The payment id given by the gateway
options.why: It is unique per transaction and present on both sides.

options.text: Our own idempotency key or merchant reference
options.why: We create it ourselves and the gateway returns it in the statement, so it matches on both sides.

options.text: The amount and the time down to the minute
options.why: Many transactions can share the same amount in the same minute.

options.text: The customer's name and the amount
options.why: The same customer can send the same amount twice, and the wrong lines will get paired.

questions.q: The nightly reconcile job crashed the server partway and stopped. It was run again in the morning. What happens in `recon_break` if UNIQUE and ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING are in place?
questions.hint: What happens when the same break tries to go in again?

options.text: Breaks already inserted are not inserted again; the new ones are
options.why: UNIQUE plus DO NOTHING makes the job safe to run again.

options.text: Every break is inserted twice
options.why: The UNIQUE constraint won't allow it.

options.text: The job stops with an error and someone has to clean the table by hand
options.why: ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING means no error is raised.

options.why: DO NOTHING means the old rows are not touched at all.

options.text: status_mismatch: a refund we never saw
options.why: The amount agrees but the status doesn't. The query compares status after amount, so this is where it lands.

options.text: amount_mismatch

questions.q: The gateway statement dates a payment 21 November, but our ledger recorded it at 11:59 p.m. on 20 November. How does the 20 November job label it?
questions.hint: The same reference is on both sides.

options.text: As a timing break: the reference matches, only the day differs
options.why: The query looks one day either side, finds the ref on the 21st, and labels it timing instead of missing. A cutoff difference is not a real error.

options.text: As missing_at_provider, because the 20 November statement has no such line
options.why: That would raise a false alarm. The join also looks at the neighboring day, where the line is found.

options.why: Ledger entries can't be changed, and the cause is the cutoff, not the date.

questions.q: The config below has a serious gap. What is it?

questions.hint: What happens when the vendor is slow?

options.text: There is no timeout or max_duration; when the vendor is slow, workers get stuck
options.why: The default wait is very long. For every vendor you must set timeout and max_duration explicitly.

options.text: `auth_bearer` should not use an env variable
options.why: Keeping the key in an env variable is the right approach; that isn't the problem.

options.text: A dot in the scoped client's name is wrong
options.why: `sms.client` is a perfectly valid name; it is injected as `$smsClient`.

questions.q: After POST /charges to the gateway, the request times out. What should the app do?
questions.hint: Do we know whether the money was taken?

options.text: Try again with a new Idempotency-Key
options.why: If the first call succeeded, a new key takes the money twice.

options.text: Show "failed" straight away and cancel the order
options.why: A timeout means "we don't know". If the money was taken, the customer pays and gets no order.

options.text: Mark the state as "unknown", then retry with the same key or check the status
options.why: Sending again with the same key won't take the money a second time, and you can also confirm the status another way.

options.text: Assume "success" and confirm the order
options.why: We don't know whether it succeeded. Assuming without knowing is also wrong.

questions.q: Which of these are good habits when setting up retries in Symfony HttpClient?
questions.hint: Think about the wait, the spreading out, and which errors are worth retrying.

options.text: Increasing the wait on each attempt (multiplier)
options.why: It gives the vendor time to recover.

options.text: Randomizing the retry timing with jitter
options.why: Not every client hits at the same instant.

options.text: Retrying on 429 and 503, but not on 400
options.why: 429 and 503 are temporary problems; a 400 means the request is wrong, and sending it again gives the same result.

options.text: Retrying every error as many times as possible with no pause
options.why: It puts the vendor under even more pressure, and a bad request is needlessly sent again and again.

questions.q: The vendor's limit is 100 calls/second. A job suddenly sent 500 calls and got many 429s. Which fix is best?
questions.hint: The problem starts on our side.

options.text: Put a token bucket limiter on our side and keep the pace at about 80/second
options.why: Staying below the limit means a 429 almost never comes, and the vendor can't block us.

options.text: Resend immediately on every 429, with no pause
options.why: That brings even more 429s and raises the risk of being blocked.

options.text: Create a second API key to get around the limit
options.why: It risks breaking the contract; the vendor can lock the account.

options.text: Raise the timeout to 60 seconds
options.why: The problem is the rate limit; a longer wait gets more workers stuck.

questions.q: A web request calls the gateway with `timeout: 3` and `max_retries: 3`. At 10 requests a second with 50 workers, the gateway dies. What happens?
questions.hint: How long can one request hold a worker, with four attempts and the waits between them?

options.text: Each request holds a worker for 15 seconds or more, so all 50 workers are stuck within about 5 seconds
options.why: 4 attempts of 3 seconds plus 3.5 seconds of waiting is about 15.5 seconds. 10 requests a second times 15 is far more than 50 workers.

options.text: Nothing; the timeout of 3 seconds protects the site
options.why: The timeout is per attempt. The retries multiply the time the worker is held.

options.text: The retries help, because the gateway recovers in time
options.why: Even if it recovers, the workers were stuck while waiting, and every page on the site suffered.

options.text: Only checkout is affected; the rest of the site stays up
options.why: Workers are shared by every page. When they are all stuck, the home page has none left.

questions.q: You send $2,000,000 a month through Acme. Its fee rises from 1.5% to 2.5%; a rival charges 1.2%. What does switching save, and what makes it easy?
questions.hint: Compare 2.5% with 1.2%, not with the old 1.5%.

options.text: $26,000 a month; with an adapter you write one class and change one alias
options.why: 1.3% of $2,000,000 is $26,000. The vendor's vocabulary lives in one adapter, so the swap is small.

options.text: $20,000 a month
options.why: That is only the rise from 1.5% to 2.5%. The saving against the rival is 2.5% minus 1.2%.

options.text: $26,000 a month, but only after rewriting every place that reads Acme's fields
options.why: That is the price of having no adapter. With one, the translation lives in a single class.

options.text: Nothing; an interface makes every vendor behave identically

options.why: With an adapter, the translation would live in one place. Without one, changing vendor means a big refactor.

options.text: No problem, a find-and-replace will do

options.text: The new vendor's SDK will adapt all of this by itself
options.why: The new SDK has its own vocabulary; the old code doesn't change by itself.

questions.q: The cron read the file at 2 a.m., but the bank was still uploading it. Which is the best prevention?

options.why: Changing the time may happen to line up with the upload, but it gives no guarantee.

options.text: Read the file if its size looks big enough

options.text: Add `sleep(60)` to the cron and wait
options.why: It's a guess; with a slow upload even 60 seconds might not be enough.

questions.q: The trailer says 2 rows, 175050 cents in total. Our own count is 2 rows, 175150 in total. What should we do?

options.text: It should use `while` instead of `foreach`

questions.q: Which of these help make a file integration safe to run again (idempotent)?
questions.hint: Think about both the file level and the row level.

options.text: A UNIQUE constraint on `(provider, sha256)`
options.why: If the same file comes a second time, it isn't even registered.

options.text: A UNIQUE on `(file_id, line_no)` in the results table
options.why: If it runs again after a crash, the same row isn't loaded a second time.

questions.q: In which situation is RPC a good fit?

options.text: Validating a card at checkout, where you need the result now
options.why: The user is waiting, and you can't go on without the answer. RPC with a timeout and retries fits.

options.text: Sending a confirmation email after an order
options.why: An email can go later; putting it on a message queue is better.

options.text: Taking in a nightly statement of 1,000,000 rows
options.why: A file transfer is cheap and a good fit here.

options.text: Telling the analytics team about an order when we aren't sure they are up
options.why: The other side may be down; with messaging our work isn't held up.

questions.q: What is the biggest risk in this code?

options.text: Our request hangs waiting for the warehouse (no timeout), and we can end up with a saved order that has no reservation
options.why: Inside RPC the work splits in two: the order is saved but the reservation isn't. With no timeout, a slow warehouse traps the worker.

options.text: `save()` shouldn't be called first
options.why: Even with the order swapped, the two jobs are still separate, and the RPC risk remains.

options.text: You can't use `getStatusCode()`
options.why: That isn't a specific problem.

options.text: There is no risk; the warehouse is always reliable
options.why: No service is always reliable.

questions.q: Which of these precautions does messaging need?
questions.hint: How many times can a queue deliver the same message?

options.text: Making the handler idempotent
options.why: A message can arrive more than once; the second time must not do the work twice.

options.text: Putting only the needed facts in the message (an id, an amount), not the whole entity
options.why: A small contract gives a looser tie, and the message doesn't break when the entity changes.

options.text: Retries and a failure transport for failed messages
options.why: Some messages fail again and again; if they are lost, the work is lost too.

options.text: Making the producer stop and wait for a reply to each message
options.why: Then it is no longer messaging; it has turned into RPC.

questions.q: An old government system wants 500,000 rows of data each night, and all they have is SFTP. Which style?
questions.hint: An outside system, big data, a delay is fine.

options.text: File transfer, with a checksum and a control total
options.why: The data is big and regular, and SFTP is the other side's only route. It becomes safe once it passes the verification gates.

options.text: One HTTP call per row
options.why: The other side doesn't offer HTTP, and 500,000 calls would be slow and expensive.

options.text: Writing directly into their database
options.why: Never touch another system's database; they wouldn't give you permission anyway.

options.text: Sending one message per row
options.why: They have no message broker, and 500,000 messages is extra trouble.

questions.q: Ryan dispatches `OrderPlaced` with Messenger, but `messenger.yaml` has no routing for it. The warehouse service is down. What happens?
questions.hint: Where does a message with no route get handled?

options.text: The message waits on a queue and the order succeeds
options.why: No queue was chosen. A queue exists only where a route sends the message to an async transport.

options.text: Messenger retries it in the background three times
options.why: Retries belong to a transport. Here nothing is on a transport, so nothing is retried.

options.text: The handler runs inside the request, fails, and the order fails with it
options.why: With no route, Messenger handles the message synchronously. It is RPC in disguise, and the warehouse's outage becomes ours.

options.text: The message is silently dropped and the order succeeds
options.why: A message with no route is not dropped. It is handled right away, inside the request.
